Solution

Register Variable
If you have a variable in your C/C++ program that you frequently access, and it's used in a tight loop, you can suggest to the compiler to keep the variable in one of the CPU's registers.
However, the variable needs to fit within a register (typically a 32-bit or 64-bit integer) and you must not take the address of the variable. Also, the compiler is free to not use a register for the variable even if you ask it to.
Example:
register int x;
static Variable
If you declare a local variable in a function as static, it means that you can preserve the value of the variable between function calls. The variable is initialized when the function is first called, but is not reset on subsequent calls.

Example:
void foo(void)
{
static int x;
...
}
Here, x is an automatic variable (since its scope is limited to the function foo()) but the storage duration of x is static, meaning that it is not destroyed and re-created when the function is exited. Instead, its lifetime is the entire execution of the program.
